name: Simple Teacher AI: tested AI ideas for teachers
description: Practical AI use cases for K-12 teachers. Each prompt was run on a sample classroom and checked by hand. The verdict says what happened.
privacy: Never put student names or identifying details into an AI tool. Use your district-approved tool.

items.title: Emergency sub plans: build them once with AI, not the night you're sick
items.takes_about: 15 min per class, once a semester
items.prompt: Act as an experienced instructional designer. Write a one-day emergency substitute plan for my [grade] [subject] class. It must need zero prep from the sub and use only paper, pencils, and what's in a typical classroom. Use my real schedule: [paste times]. Use my real routines: [attendance, bathroom, lining up, quiet signal]. If I didn't give you a routine, write "ASK THE TEACHER NEXT DOOR" instead of making one up. Include: a review activity on [recent topic] with an answer key, a quiet independent task, and a 5-minute filler activity. Before you finish, solve every problem and puzzle yourself and make sure each one has exactly one correct answer.
items.why_it_works: Giving it your real schedule and routines, and telling it not to invent the rest, is what makes the plan usable by a stranger.

sources.title: Edutopia
Ditch That Textbook

items.title: A lesson hook in 30 seconds
items.tool: Gemini in Google Classroom (also any chatbot)
items.prompt: My [grade] students are learning [specific goal, e.g. "how to find the area of a rectangle"]. Give me 5 ways to open this lesson in under 3 minutes: one question, one quick demo, one puzzle, one connection to something kids care about, and one "what's wrong with this picture." Each one must lead straight into the goal, not just be fun. No prep longer than 2 minutes.
items.why_it_works: Naming the exact goal keeps the hooks from being cute but off-topic. Gemini in Classroom has "craft a compelling hook" as a built-in starter prompt, including on the phone app (teachers 18+, and your district admin has to turn it on).

sources.title: Google Workspace Updates, June 2026

items.title: Turn a lesson into a slide deck draft
items.prompt: Make a 10-slide deck teaching [specific goal] to [grade] students, using this content from my curriculum: [paste]. One idea per slide, big text. Include one worked example, a check-for-understanding question every 3 slides, and short speaker notes telling me what to say. Final slide: an exit question.
items.why_it_works: You get the skeleton in minutes. Pasting your own curriculum content keeps it from teaching the topic a different way than your program does.

sources.title: Google Workspace Updates, June 2026

items.title: Know the likely mix-ups before you teach
items.prompt: I'm about to teach [topic] to [grade] students. Suggest 5 mix-ups students are likely to have. For each one, give the wrong idea in a kid's words, why it makes sense to a kid, and one quick question I can ask to find out who has it.
items.why_it_works: Knowing where kids will go wrong changes how you teach it. Treat the list as a brainstorm, not research, and check it against what you've seen in your room.

sources.title: Google Workspace Updates
research on AI-written math questions (arXiv)

items.title: Kid-friendly "I can" statements from any standard
items.prompt: Rewrite this standard as 2-3 "I can" statements a [grade] student would understand. Use words a [age]-year-old knows, but keep the same skill and the same level of challenge. Don't make it easier than the standard. Use a real example instead of letters or symbols from the standard. Standard: [paste standard]
items.why_it_works: Standards are written for adults. The "don't make it easier" line matters: kid-friendly rewrites tend to quietly drop the hard part.

sources.title: Teaching Channel, 65 AI Prompts for Lesson Planning (PDF)

items.title: One passage, three versions
items.verdict_detail: better, but still needs your edit
items.prompt: Make two more versions of this passage for my [grade] class. Version A: short, simple sentences and hard words explained in plain words, for students who find it too hard. Keep it about the same length as the original. Version B: richer vocabulary and one extra detail, for students who find it too easy. Keep every fact and idea in both, in the same order, so the whole class can discuss it together. After each version, list what you changed. [paste passage]
items.why_it_works: Same content, same discussion, different access. Doing passages first and questions second gives better results.

sources.title: The Animated Teacher

items.title: Decodable text generator: a custom decodable story in 10 minutes
items.verdict_detail: better, but you must check every word
items.prompt: Write a short decodable story for first graders. Target pattern: [e.g. short o]. Use only these high-frequency words: [list]. Every other word must use patterns we've learned: [list]. Write it about [something your class did this week]. 6-8 sentences. Every sentence must make sense to a 6-year-old and the story needs a tiny beginning, middle, and end. After the story, check every single word one at a time against the rules (including names and small words) and list any word that breaks them.
items.why_it_works: Kids read more when the story is about their world. But this is the card where you most need to check the AI's work.

sources.title: ASCD, How to Create Custom Decodable Texts in Minutes

items.title: Word problem generator: problems about what your class cares about
items.prompt: Write 8 [grade] word problems practicing [skill, e.g. two-step multiplication]. Base them on things my class is into right now: [Pokemon, recess soccer, the class fish, Minecraft]. Same difficulty as these examples from my curriculum: [paste 1-2 problems]. Vary the wording and question so the problems don't all follow the same pattern. Include an answer key.
items.why_it_works: Same math, more buy-in. List class interests, never individual students.

sources.title: Rowan University study on interest-based reading texts (3 students, so a promising idea, not proof)

items.title: Make the directions readable for everyone
items.prompt: Rewrite these directions for a student who [is still learning English / reads below grade level]. Don't change what the task asks them to do. Use simple everyday words. Keep the school words they need to learn (like "quote") and explain each one in parentheses the first time. Number the steps, one action per step, bold the key verb. [paste directions]
items.why_it_works: A lot of "I don't get it" is the directions, not the work. Pick one need at a time: an English learner and a struggling reader need different fixes.

sources.title: OpenAI Edu Prompt newsletter, Issue 4

items.title: Plan reteach groups from your quiz results
items.verdict_detail: worked first try. One of the best in the batch
items.prompt: I gave a [topic] quiz to [number] students. Here is how many missed each question and the skill each question tests: [paste]. Suggest 3-4 reteach groups by skill, a likely reason students missed those questions (a guess, not a diagnosis), and a 10-minute reteach plan for each group.
items.why_it_works: Turns a gradebook column into a plan for tomorrow's small groups, without any student-level data leaving your computer.

sources.title: OpenAI Edu Prompt newsletter, Issue 4
US Dept. of Education: what counts as de-identified

items.title: Exit ticket examples with answers, and what a wrong answer means
items.prompt: Write 5 exit tickets for this [grade] lesson goal: [goal]. Each one should take under 2 minutes and show me whether the student got the main idea. For each, include the answer, a short worked solution, and what a wrong answer might mean (a guess I should check, not a diagnosis).
items.why_it_works: "What a wrong answer might mean" is the key line. It turns an exit ticket into tomorrow's plan.

sources.title: Learning in Hand (Tony Vincent): Designing and analyzing exit tickets with AI

items.title: Multiple choice where the wrong answers mean something
items.prompt: Write 5 multiple-choice questions on [topic] for [grade]. Mistakes I actually see in my class: [list, or "none yet"]. Each wrong answer must come from one specific mistake. For every question, show the worked solution, and next to each wrong answer, name the mistake that produces it. Write fractions and math as plain text, like 1/2, so I can paste them into a document.
items.why_it_works: If you know why a kid picked B, you know what to reteach. Giving it the mistakes you really see makes the wrong answers much better.

sources.title: Math question generation research (EDM 2024)

items.title: A rubric from your assignment directions
items.prompt: Make a 4-level rubric for this assignment. Grade only these learning goals: [list, 4 max]. For each level, describe what I would actually see in the student's work, not vague words like "shows understanding." Then make a student-friendly checklist version using "I" statements. [paste assignment directions]
items.why_it_works: You get the grading tool and the student self-check in one shot.

sources.title: Teacher workshop study on AI rubrics (arXiv, 2026)

items.title: First-draft feedback on writing, using your rubric
items.takes_about: 1 min per paper plus your review
items.prompt: You're an experienced [grade] teacher. Here is the assignment: [paste directions]. Using only this rubric: [paste 3-5 criteria], give feedback on the anonymous student writing below. Format: one specific strength with a quote copied exactly from the writing, one next step, one question to push their thinking. Only comment on what is actually in the writing. Under 80 words. Kind and direct.
items.why_it_works: A fixed format and a short rubric keep the AI on track. Requiring an exact quote makes it harder for the AI to praise something that isn't there.

sources.title: EdSurge: teachers reflect on an AI writing rubric tool

items.title: A report card comment bank (no student data needed)
items.prompt: Write a bank of report card comments for [grade] [subject]. For each of these skills: [list 5-6 skills], write one comment for "exceeding," "meeting," "approaching," and "needs support." Warm, specific, under 30 words each, written to parents, with [Name] as a placeholder. Write the way you'd talk to a parent at pickup: no education jargon, and don't start every comment the same way. Each "approaching" and "needs support" comment should include one thing families can do at home.
items.why_it_works: You build the bank once, then pick and tweak per student. No student information ever goes into the AI.

sources.title: The Animated Teacher
Edutopia

items.title: Weekly family newsletter from your scribbled notes
items.prompt: Turn these notes into a short, warm weekly newsletter for families of my [grade] class. Sections: what we learned, what's coming up, one way to help at home. Under 200 words. Sound like a real teacher, not a company. Don't add any events or dates that aren't in my notes. Notes: [paste bullet points]
items.why_it_works: The hard part (knowing what happened this week) is yours. The AI handles the writing.

sources.title: eSpark

items.title: Translate a family message, carefully
items.prompt: Translate this message into [language] for families. Keep it warm and simple and avoid idioms. Keep every date, time, number, and thing families need to do exactly the same. Then, in English, list any sentence you weren't sure how to translate, and any sentence you changed or softened instead of translating word for word.
items.why_it_works: Gets the message to families who'd otherwise miss it. Quality varies by language (Spanish is strong, some others less so).

sources.title: GovTech

items.title: Rehearse a hard parent conference out loud
items.verdict_detail: opening works; full conversation not tested yet
items.prompt: I'm a [grade] teacher. Play a frustrated parent who thinks I'm being unfair to their child about [general situation, no names]. Push back the way a real upset parent would. Say one thing at a time and wait for my answer. When I say STOP, step out of character and tell me what I did well and where I got defensive.
items.why_it_works: Saying the hard sentence out loud once makes it much easier the second time.

sources.title: Education Week, May 2026

items.title: Cool down an email before you hit send
items.prompt: I'm a teacher replying to a parent. Make this email calm, kind, and clear without losing what I need to say. Cut anything that sounds defensive. Keep it short. [paste your cleaned-up draft]
items.why_it_works: The 9pm angry draft is honest. The calm version is the one you'll be glad you sent.

sources.title: eSpark

items.title: Explain school jargon to families in plain English
items.prompt: Explain these terms to a parent with no education background, one or two sentences each, friendly tone: [e.g. "benchmark assessment," "Lexile level," "RTI Tier 2," "accommodation vs. modification"].
items.why_it_works: Use general terms only, never a specific student's plan. Make it once and reuse it at every conference.

sources.title: Truth for Teachers

items.title: An assembly ate 20 minutes. Shrink tomorrow's lesson.
items.prompt: Here is my [length]-minute lesson plan for [grade] [subject]: [paste plan]. An assembly just cut it to [new length] minutes. Rewrite it to fit. Keep the learning goal and enough independent practice for me to see who got it. Cut or shorten everything else. Give me the new plan with minutes for each part that add up to exactly [new length], then a list of what you cut and where I could fit it later this week. Don't add anything new.
items.why_it_works: Telling it what must survive (the goal and the practice you learn from) stops it from cutting the wrong part.

sources.title: Tes, on the Education Endowment Foundation ChatGPT trial

items.title: Worked examples practice page: one solved, then one for them
items.prompt: I'm teaching [skill] to [grade] students. Make a practice page that alternates: a worked example, then a similar problem for students, then another worked example, then a similar problem, 4 pairs in all. Each worked example shows every step with one short sentence saying why. Make the third and fourth worked examples only half done, so students finish the last steps. Get a little harder each pair. Give each student problem a different answer from the worked example right before it, so nobody can just copy the answer. Write math as plain text, like 3 x 4. Solve every problem yourself, make sure each has exactly one correct answer, and give me an answer key at the end. In the key, show each pair's two answers side by side, and change any student problem whose answer matches its example.
items.why_it_works: Alternating a solved example with a problem to try is one of the few practice-page moves with research behind it.

sources.title: IES practice guide, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (Recommendation 2, PDF)

items.title: Hear the hardest questions before your students ask them
items.prompt: Here is what I'm teaching tomorrow: [paste lesson or reading]. My students are in [grade]. Play a curious, skeptical student in my class and list the 10 hardest questions students this age really ask about it. Mix "why" questions, "but what about..." questions, and questions that come from a real mix-up. For each one, give me a short, true answer I could say to a [age]-year-old. If a question has no simple answer, say so and suggest what I can say instead.
items.why_it_works: The questions that stump you are rarely the ones in the teacher's guide.

sources.title: The 74, "11 AI prompts every teacher should know" (via Stacker)

items.title: Find the blind spots in your lesson plan
items.prompt: Here is my lesson plan: [paste]. My class: [grade, class size, general needs like "6 English learners, 2 students who need read-aloud support," no names]. Be a blunt, experienced teacher reviewing it. Find up to 5 real problems: where kids will get lost, directions that could be read two ways, timing that won't work, anything that leaves some students out, and whether the exit check actually measures the goal. If there are fewer than 5, say so instead of inventing more. For each, quote the line from my plan and give a specific fix. Keep definite problems separate from questions you'd want to ask me. Don't rewrite the whole plan, and don't praise it.
items.why_it_works: Asking for problems (not a rewrite) keeps your plan yours. "Quote the line" forces it to point at something real instead of giving generic advice.

sources.title: The 74, "11 AI prompts every teacher should know" (via Stacker)

items.title: Plan the stopping points for a read-aloud
items.prompt: Here is a story I'm reading aloud to my [grade] class: [paste the text, or today's pages]. Pick 4 stopping points. For each, quote the exact sentence I should stop after, and give one turn-and-talk question that makes partners think (predict, infer, or explain a character's choice), not just recall. Add one model answer so I can show what a good answer sounds like. Each question and answer can only use what has happened in the story so far, so nothing gets spoiled. Only use what's in the text I pasted, and quote it word for word.
items.why_it_works: Planning where to stop is what turns a read-aloud into a lesson. "Quote it word for word" lets you find each stop in the book in seconds, and lets you catch it if it invents a line.

sources.title: Edutopia, Building Better Readers With Scaffolded Read Alouds (video)
Edutopia, Turn and Talk anchor chart (PDF)

items.title: Frayer model vocabulary: kid-friendly definitions, examples, and nonexamples
items.prompt: Here are this week's vocabulary words from our [grade] [subject or book]: [list]. For each word, write: a student-friendly definition in everyday words a [age]-year-old knows (don't use the word itself or a harder word to explain it), one example sentence from a kid's life, one nonexample (something that is NOT this word, and why), and a quick yes/no question I can ask the class to check understanding. Keep the meaning the book uses: [paste the sentence from the book for each word, if you have it].
items.why_it_works: Dictionary definitions rarely work for kids. Explaining a word in everyday language, then showing what it is and isn't, is the core of robust vocabulary teaching.

sources.title: Reading Rockets, Bringing Words to Life (Beck, McKeown, Kucan)
National Center on Improving Literacy, Explicit Vocabulary Instruction (PDF)

items.title: A 10-minute reteach that comes at it a different way
items.prompt: [Number] of my [grade] students still can't [skill] after today's lesson. I taught it by [how you taught it]. The most common mistake was [describe it, e.g. "subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger one in each column"]. Plan a 10-minute small-group reteach that comes at it a different way: different materials or a picture or model, not the same explanation slower. Use only things found in a typical classroom. Include what I say, what students do, 3 practice problems with answers, and one final check question that shows whether the mistake is fixed. Write math as plain text. Solve every problem yourself.
items.why_it_works: Saying how you already taught it is the key line. Without it, you get your own lesson back, louder.

sources.title: Achieve the Core, Using Exit Tickets Strategically

items.title: Same goal, two ways in: make practice easier to start without making it easier
items.prompt: Here is a practice page my [grade] students do: [paste]. Make two more versions. Version 1, for students who struggle to get started: same goal and the same kind of thinking, with supports like a worked first problem, a hint box, or a number line. Don't swap hard problems for easier ones. For each support, say whether it does any thinking students should do themselves. Version 2, for students who finish fast: same goal, but problems that ask them to explain, compare, or create, not just more of the same. Write math as plain text. Solve every problem yourself, give answer keys, and list what you changed in each version.
items.why_it_works: The usual "easier version" quietly swaps in easier problems, so some kids never practice the real skill.

sources.title: The 74, "11 AI prompts every teacher should know" (via Stacker)

items.title: Sentence frames for discussion, at three levels
items.prompt: We're discussing [question] in [grade] [subject]. Write sentence frames students can use to answer, at three levels: starting (short frames with a word bank), building (full-sentence frames), and stretching (frames for giving a reason and evidence, or disagreeing politely). Keep frames open enough that students can answer in different ways. Put the content words students need in the word bank. Then write one model answer using the "building" frames so I can say it aloud first.
items.why_it_works: Frames let English learners (and quiet kids) focus on the idea instead of hunting for the sentence.

sources.title: Colorín Colorado, Sentence Frames and Sentence Starters

items.title: Fluency passages with word counts, about anything your class likes
items.prompt: Write a [number]-word fluency passage for [grade] students about [topic], at a [grade] reading level. Vary the sentence lengths like a real story: some short, some long. Put one sentence per row, and at the end of each row write the running total of words so far in brackets, like [12]. Count hyphenated words and numbers as one word each. When you're done, count the whole passage again word by word and fix any total that's wrong. Then give me 3 short comprehension questions.
items.why_it_works: Timed repeated reading needs a passage with running word counts so you can score words correct per minute fast.

sources.title: Reading Rockets, Timed Repeated Readings

items.title: Early finisher choice board that still practices the skill
items.prompt: Make a 3x3 choice board for [grade] students who finish early in [subject]. Every square must practice [this week's skill], not just keep them busy. Each square needs directions a student can follow alone without asking me, using only paper, pencil, and what's in a typical classroom. Mix it up: some drawing, some writing, some puzzles, one that makes them explain their thinking. Solve every problem or puzzle yourself and make sure each has exactly one answer (or say that it's open-ended). Add an answer key for anything with a right answer.
items.why_it_works: "Every square must practice the skill" is the line that turns busywork into practice.

sources.title: Edutopia, fast finishers: keeping students in any grade engaged

items.title: Find the mistake: realistic wrong answers for kids to fix
items.prompt: I'm teaching [skill] to [grade] students. Write 5 examples of student work that each contain one realistic mistake that kids at this age actually make. Don't label the mistakes in the examples. Make each mistake different. After the examples, give me a teacher key that names each mistake, explains why a student would make it, and shows the correct answer. Write math as plain text. Check your key against your examples one by one.
items.why_it_works: Kids learn a lot from finding errors, but you can't put a real student's wrong work on the board.

sources.title: The 74, "11 AI prompts every teacher should know" (via Stacker)

items.title: Sort a stack of math exit tickets by mistake
items.prompt: Here are [number] exit ticket answers from my [grade] class, numbered, no names. The question was: [paste question]. The correct answer is: [answer]. Group the answers by what you can see in them: correct, correct answer with a small error, and each kind of wrong answer. Use a "can't tell" group when an answer doesn't show enough to know what the student was thinking, and give me one follow-up question I could ask those students. Every ticket number must appear exactly once. Then suggest a 5-minute warm-up for tomorrow that targets the biggest group of wrong answers. [paste answers]
items.why_it_works: Sorting by the kind of mistake, not just right or wrong, tells you what to reteach.

sources.title: Achieve the Core, Using Exit Tickets Strategically

items.title: Free social story generator for a classroom routine
items.prompt: Write a short class story to teach my [grade] class the routine for [routine, e.g. "a fire drill"]. Use our real steps: [list the steps]. Write it in first person ("I"), present tense, in short sentences a [age]-year-old can read. Describe what happens, how it might feel (loud, surprising), and what I can do, using calm, positive words. Say what to do, not just what not to do. 8 to 12 sentences. Don't add steps I didn't give you. After the story, list situations my steps don't cover that a student might worry about (for example, being out of the room when the alarm rings), as questions for me.
items.why_it_works: Short stories that describe a situation and what to do are called social narratives.

sources.title: AFIRM (UNC), Social Narratives module
Chalkbeat, on the Common Sense Media AI teacher assistant report
Common Sense Media, AI Teacher Assistants risk assessment

items.title: A study buddy that's told not to do the homework
items.tool: a Gem in Google Classroom (or a custom GPT or Project for older students, if your district allows it)
items.verdict_detail: works after a fix (tested with a single message and one pushback, not a full conversation)
items.prompt: You are a study buddy for [grade] students learning [unit or topic]. Never give the final answer to a homework or practice problem, and never write sentences or paragraphs a student could turn in. Instead, ask one question at a time to help the student take the next step, give a hint, or show a similar example with different numbers. Before you send a hint, check that it leads to the right answer for the student's exact problem. If the student asks you to just give the answer, kindly say no and offer a hint. Keep replies under 4 sentences and use words a [age]-year-old knows. If a student shares personal information or says something worrying, tell them to talk to their teacher or a trusted adult. Don't ask for names.
items.why_it_works: The rule against writing turn-in sentences matters as much as the no-answers rule.

sources.title: Google Classroom Help: Create and assign Gemini Notebook and Gems
Ditch That Textbook, Gemini Gems in the classroom

items.title: Tell students exactly how they may use AI on this assignment
items.tool: Any chatbot, or the free Transparency Support site
items.prompt: Write a short "How you may use AI on this assignment" box for my [grade] students, to paste at the top of the directions. The assignment is: [describe]. AI is allowed for: [e.g. brainstorming topics, checking spelling]. AI is not allowed for: [e.g. writing any sentences you turn in]. Use "you can" and "you can't" lists, plain words, under 100 words. Don't add rules I didn't give you. End with one sentence students fill in to tell me how they used AI.
items.why_it_works: "Don't use AI" is hard to enforce and "use AI responsibly" means nothing to a 12-year-old.

sources.title: Transparency Support
Learning in Hand apps (Tony Vincent)

items.title: Catch the AI's mistakes: a 10-minute AI literacy warm-up
items.prompt: Here is a short text from our [grade] unit on [topic]. Treat it as the only source of facts: [paste a paragraph from your curriculum]. Rewrite it as a 6-8 sentence paragraph for students and change exactly 3 facts, one per sentence, so they no longer match the text. Every other sentence must match the text. After the paragraph, give me a teacher key: quote each changed sentence, say what's wrong, and quote the line from my text that proves it.
items.why_it_works: Students practice checking a confident-sounding paragraph against a trusted source, and they review your unit while they hunt.

sources.title: NCWIT, AI Detectives
Common Sense Education, AI literacy lessons

items.title: Tell families how your class uses AI, in plain words
items.prompt: Write a short note to families of my [grade] class explaining how we use AI this year. Facts: [e.g. "I use AI to help plan lessons and make practice pages, and I check everything it makes"; "students can use Gemini in Google Classroom for study help on some assignments"; "students may not use AI to write work they turn in"; "student names and grades never go into AI tools"]. Use only these facts. Don't add promises or details I didn't give you. Talk like you would at pickup, not like a district memo. Under 200 words. End by inviting questions.
items.why_it_works: Families are hearing about AI in schools from the news. A short, honest note from you, before they ask, builds more trust than a policy link.

sources.title: Google Workspace Updates, August 4, 2026 (Gemini in Classroom for students)

items.title: Check your unit's order for missing steps
items.prompt: Here is the lesson-by-lesson order for my [grade] [subject] unit on [topic]: [paste the list of lessons, one line each]. Check the order like an experienced [subject] teacher. Find up to 5 places where a lesson needs a skill my students haven't been taught yet in this unit, or where two lessons should switch places. If there are fewer than 5, say so instead of inventing more. For each one, name the lessons involved, say which skill is missing or out of order, and give one specific fix (move a lesson, or add a short mini-lesson). Assume students know what a typical [grade] student learned in earlier grades, and list what you assumed. Don't rewrite the whole unit.
items.why_it_works: A unit can look fine lesson by lesson and still ask kids to use a skill two days before you teach it.

sources.title: Microsoft Education Blog, What's New in Microsoft EDU, October 2026
Achieve the Core, Coherence Map (how math standards build on each other)

items.title: Lab safety check: find the hazards in a lab procedure before students run it
items.takes_about: 5 min, plus time with the safety data sheets
items.prompt: Here is a lab procedure my [grade] [course] students will do: [paste the procedure, including chemicals, concentrations, and amounts]. Act as a careful high school lab safety reviewer. List every real safety problem you find, most dangerous first: missing protective equipment, steps in an unsafe order, chemicals that shouldn't be mixed or heated, missing cleanup or disposal steps, and directions students could misread. Don't pad the list with steps that are fine. Never tell me the procedure is safe: a qualified person at my school decides that. If you find no problems, say "no problems found." For each problem, quote the step, say in plain words what could go wrong, and give a specific fix. Then list what you couldn't check from the text alone (like ventilation, eyewash access, or supervision), and what I should look up in the safety data sheet for each chemical. Don't make up chemical facts: if you aren't sure about a hazard, say so.
items.why_it_works: Quoting the step makes it point at your procedure instead of reciting general lab rules.

sources.title: American Chemical Society, Guidelines for Chemical Laboratory Safety in Secondary Schools (PDF)
ACS, middle and high school chemistry safety resources

items.title: Claim, evidence, reasoning example: a strong and a weak CER paragraph from your own lab data
items.prompt: My [grade] science students are writing claim, evidence, reasoning (CER) paragraphs to answer this question: [question]. Here is the data from our lab: [paste your data table]. If the data don't clearly support one claim, or a result doesn't fit the pattern, tell me that first, and don't change or leave out any numbers. Then write two model answers to show the class: one strong, one weak but typical. Use only the numbers in my data, copied exactly. In the strong one, the reasoning must explain why the evidence supports the claim using this science idea: [idea]. Don't just repeat the data. In the weak one, make the mistakes students this age really make (like a claim with no data, or reasoning that just restates the evidence). Label each part [Claim], [Evidence], [Reasoning]. After the weak one, list its mistakes so I can have students find them first. Keep each paragraph under [80] words.
items.why_it_works: Reasoning is the part students find hardest, the "why does this evidence matter?" step.

sources.title: Edutopia, Teaching CER in Middle School Science With a 5-Day Structure

items.title: Number talks for the week: one problem a day, with the strategies kids will use
items.takes_about: 5 min, plus 5 min to check the steps
items.prompt: Plan 5 number talks for my [grade] class, one per day, 5 to 10 minutes each. We are working on [skill, e.g. "adding two-digit numbers in your head"]. For each day give me: one problem to show the class, 2 to 4 strategies students this age might use, each written step by step the way a student would say it, one common wrong answer and the thinking behind it, and one question I can ask to push the discussion. Pick numbers that make more than one strategy useful. Write math as plain text, like 38 + 25. Each strategy must work cleanly with that day's numbers, with no false starts. The common wrong answer must come from a real misunderstanding kids this age have (like place value or forgetting to regroup), not a basic fact error like 4 + 5 = 11. Do the mistaken steps yourself to make sure they lead to that wrong answer. Solve every problem and check every step of every strategy yourself.
items.why_it_works: A number talk only works if you can hear a strategy and recognize it fast.

items.title: Guided notes template from your own slides
items.prompt: Here are my notes for tomorrow's [grade] [subject] lesson: [paste your slides or notes]. Turn them into a one-page guided notes handout. Keep my order and my wording. Replace about [10] key words with blanks: only words that matter (vocabulary, key numbers, causes and effects), never small words like "the" or "is." Each blank must be a word or short phrase that appears in my notes, so students can find it while I teach. If you blank a word, blank it everywhere it appears on the handout except the title, so the page doesn't give away its own answers. Number every blank. Make every blank the same length, like ________, so the length doesn't give the answer away. Add 2 short "In your own words" questions at the end. Then give me an answer key that lists every numbered blank in order with the exact word from my notes. Don't add facts that aren't in my notes.
items.why_it_works: Guided notes let students listen instead of copying every word, and the blanks keep them following along.

sources.title: Modern Classrooms Project, A Guide to Guided Notes

items.title: Spaced review warm-ups from what you've already taught
items.takes_about: 5 min, plus 5 min to check the key
items.prompt: Here are the topics my [grade] [subject] class has learned so far this year, with the week we taught each: [list]. Make [number] days of 3-question review warm-ups. Each day, mix topics from different times: one from the last 2 weeks, one from 3 to 6 weeks ago, and one from earlier than that. Don't put the same topic on two days in a row. When a topic comes back, ask about it a different way than before (for example a word problem, finding a mistake, or working backward), so the questions don't all follow the same pattern. Questions should make students recall or use the idea, not just recognize it, so no multiple choice and no true or false. Write math as plain text, like 3/4. Solve every question yourself and make sure each has exactly one correct answer. Then give me a separate answer key, and a table showing which topic appears on which day so I can check the spacing.
items.why_it_works: Coming back to old topics after a gap, and making students pull the answer from memory, are two of the best-supported study moves in learning research.

sources.title: IES practice guide, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (Recommendations 1 and 5, PDF)

items.title: Study guide template that matches your test without giving it away
items.takes_about: 5 min, plus 5 min to work the problems
items.prompt: My [grade] [subject] class has a test on [unit]. Here is what the test covers: [list each skill and the kind of question, e.g. "solve two-step equations (4 short problems)"]. Make a one-page study guide students can use at home. For each skill: one sentence on what to remember, one worked example, and 2 practice problems like the test but not copies. Put all the answers in a separate answer section at the bottom. Write math as plain text, like 2x + 3 = 11. Solve every problem yourself and make sure each has exactly one correct answer. Only use the skills I listed: don't add skills that aren't on the test.
items.why_it_works: Paste the list of what the test covers, not the test itself, and the guide can't leak your questions.

sources.title: IES practice guide, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (Recommendation 5, PDF)

items.title: Primary source comparison questions with a quote-proof answer key
items.takes_about: 5 min, plus 5 min to check the quotes
items.prompt: Here are two primary sources my [grade] [subject] class is comparing. Document A: [title, author, date, and the text]. Document B: [title, author, date, and the text]. Treat these two texts as the only sources. Write 6 questions that make students compare them: 2 about what each document says, 2 about how they are alike or different, and 2 about each author's purpose or point of view. Every question must be answerable from the two texts. Then give me an answer key that quotes the exact words from the documents that support each answer, word for word. If a question needs outside knowledge, label it "needs background" and say what students need to know.
items.why_it_works: You choose and paste the documents, so the AI is working from real sources.

sources.title: Education Week, In Social Studies, Does AI Shortcut Historical Thinking or Deepen It? (October 2026)

items.title: Move the thinking where you can see it: redesign an assignment students could hand to a chatbot
items.prompt: Here is an assignment for my [grade] [subject] class: [paste the directions and due date]. Students could hand most of it to a chatbot. Redesign it so more of the thinking happens where I can see it, without making it longer for students. Keep the learning goal, the final product, and the assignment's requirements the same. I teach [number] students, so keep the added grading under [number] minutes total. Suggest up to 4 changes, like a short in-class step, a checkpoint I grade, a quick conversation, or a choice that uses something only my class did. For each change, say how many minutes of class time it takes and how many minutes of my grading time it adds. Don't claim any change makes cheating impossible. Then rewrite the directions with the changes in, in plain words students can follow. Copy my requirements into the new directions word for word and don't add any. After the directions, list every requirement you changed or added, or write "none."
items.why_it_works: No assignment is AI-proof, but grading the steps along the way, not just the final product, makes the steps worth doing.

sources.title: Ditch That Textbook, Is AI doing too much of your students' classwork?

items.title: National History Day banned generative AI. Sort what's allowed for your students.
items.prompt: Here is National History Day's AI policy: [paste the policy text from NHD's AI guidance]. My [grade] students keep asking whether specific tools are OK for their NHD projects. Sort each of these into "Allowed," "Not allowed," or "Ask NHD," using only the policy I pasted: [list, e.g. "Grammarly rewriting a sentence," "Google Translate on a Spanish-language source"]. For each, quote the line from the policy that decides it. If the policy doesn't clearly decide it, put it in "Ask NHD" and say what's unclear. Then turn the result into a half-page student handout in plain words.
items.why_it_works: As of October 1, 2026, National History Day says students "may not use generative AI for research, analysis, design, or creation of their projects," and breaking the rule may mean disqualification.

items.title: Guided Learning in Google Classroom: write the one source Gemini will teach from
items.tool: Gemini in Google Classroom, plus any chatbot to draft the source
items.verdict_detail: worked first try (we tested the prompt that drafts the source in a plain chat, not Guided Learning itself)
items.prompt: I'm making a one-page study source for a Guided Learning activity in Google Classroom. Gemini will tutor my [grade] students using this page, so it must be correct and complete. Topic: [skill]. Here is how I teach it: [paste your steps, vocabulary, and one example]. Write the page with: the goal in one sentence, key vocabulary with kid-friendly definitions, the steps in the order I teach them, 2 worked examples with every step shown, the 3 most common mistakes and how to fix each, and 3 practice problems with answers. Use my method and my words, not a different method. Write math as plain text, like 3/4. Solve every problem yourself and make sure each has exactly one correct answer. Then list anything you added that wasn't in what I gave you.
items.why_it_works: Rolling out since November 3, 2026, you can attach a Guided Learning activity to any Google Classroom assignment.
